newsitem.title: UK: Northern Ireland sways between hope and fear.
newsitem.headline: Northern Ireland sways between hope and fear.

text.p: Two days after IRA bombers hit the top British army base in Northern Ireland, the war-scarred province swayed on Wednesday between fears of new violence and hope that Loyalist guerrillas would resist the urge to hit back.

In the pro-British Protestant heartland of the Shankill Road, where Union Jack flags hang above doorways and even the kerbstones are painted red, white and blue, there were angry calls for swift, though unspecified, retribution from Britain.
"It's time Britain took a stand -- they have to be the ones that enforce law and order," said one middle-aged woman.
Her male companion wanted "the British government to go and clean them all out".

For all their fury at the Irish Republican Army (IRA), however, Protestants were praying their own guerrillas would not end a two-year ceasefire and reignite the savage civil war that claimed over 3,000 lives in 25 years.

Leaders of Protestant guerrilla groups were reported to be meeting within the next few days to decide their response. Their silence so far has left Northern Irish people guessing whether the three-year peace process sponsored by Britain and Ireland is at an end.

"I think it's quite obvious it (Monday's attack) was just a ploy to get the loyalists involved," said James Duffy, secretary of the Shankill Road branch of the Ulster Democratic Party, the political arm of the outlawed Loyalist Ulster Defence Association. "Nobody wants a resumption of strife," he said.

The bombing of the army's Lisburn barracks, 10 miles (16 km) from Belfast, was the IRA's first attack in Northern Ireland since it ended a 17-month ceasefire in February with a huge blast in east London. Thirty one people were injured at Lisburn, at least four seriously.

It was a dark hour for the province, which had begun to blossom in two years of peace. Though fighting has stopped between pro-British Protestants and Catholics seeking a united Ireland, their diehard rivalry is still as much in evidence as ever.
Almost every gable end along the Shankill Road is painted with giant, lurid tributes to dead loyalist guerrillas.
Barriers erected at the height of "the Troubles" between the Shankill Road and the Catholic Falls Road to prevent hit-and-run raids by Protestant and Catholic guerrillas are still in place.

An elderly man clutching his granddaughter's hand said he hoped the Lisburn attack was a one-off by the IRA, merely aimed at pressuring Britain into allowing the group's political arm, Sinn Fein, into peace talks.
"It was the first and I hope it will be the last," he said.
He was standing opposite a fishmonger's shop where 10 people died in 1993 in an IRA bombing.

A few yards (metres) down the road, a greengrocer's shop marks an historic point in the province's recent history. U.S. President Bill Clinton wandered in there last December to buy apples during his triumphant visit to Northern Ireland, then at the height of optimism that its troubles were over.
In the Catholic Springfield Road, it is the Irish tricolour flag that hangs above shops and homes, but few here were ready to condone the IRA's action in Lisburn.
"I don't understand their mentality," said one young man in a check shirt. "I just hope it's a spectacular intended to get the British government sitting up and listening again."
For one couple with two small children, the London blast in February which signalled the end of the IRA ceasefire was the final straw. They decided to move south to Ireland.
Their two-year-old son, born at the start of the truce, has recently been fascinated by the sight of armed British soldiers patrolling the streets again for the first time since 1994.
"We don't want him to grow up with that," his mother said.
